alignment.note: Greek uses the substantivised article οἱ ('they/the ones'), Syriac the independent demonstrative pronoun ܗܢܘܢ, and the Vulgate a relative pronoun Qui that subordinates the entire clause. All three resume the subject of the preceding verse but through distinct syntactic means.

Greek connective καί here functions adversatively ('but'), matched by the Syriac postpositive particle ܕܝܢ. The Vulgate carries no separate adversative particle, the relative Qui already supplying the connection.

Greek expresses 'having taken him' with an aorist participle plus accusative pronoun (λαβόντες αὐτόν), and the Vulgate parallels this with the perfect passive participle apprehensum eum. Syriac lacks any equivalent of 'taking', folding the action directly into the finite verb ܡܚܐܘܗܝ with a suffixed object pronoun.
ἔδειραν / ܡܚܐܘܗܝ / ceciderunt — 'they beat (him)'; the Syriac finite verb already bears the suffixed object aligned in the previous group.
ἀπέστειλαν / ܘܫܕܪܘܗܝ / dimiserunt — 'they sent (him) away'; the Syriac form carries both the conjunction ('and') and the suffixed object pronoun within a single inflected verb.

Greek κενόν and Latin vacuum render 'empty(-handed)' as a single predicate adjective, while Syriac introduces a circumstantial clause headed by ܟܕ ('while/being') plus ܣܦܝܩ ('empty'). The Syriac is semantically equivalent but syntactically a state-of-being subclause rather than a bare predicative.
